questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Membrane Structure Decides Transport
questions.learningObjective: connect bilayer structure to which solutes cross freely
questions.stem: A cell membrane is described as a double layer of molecules with water on both sides. Which statement about what can cross that layer unassisted is correct?

options.text: Small nonpolar molecules pass through, while ions and polar ones cannot
Ions pass through, while small nonpolar molecules cannot cross at all
options.misconception: reverses which class of solute crosses freely

options.text: Every solute passes freely, since gaps open between the molecules
options.misconception: believes the bilayer is a loose sieve of open pores

options.text: Only sugars pass, since their hydroxyl groups bond to the water
options.misconception: makes water-facing groups the route into the cell

questions.explanation: The interior of the layer is a region of carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen bonds that water-hating solutes cannot dissolve in, so small nonpolar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide slide through while ions and large polar molecules cannot, and those need a protein. The tempting belief that ions pass freely fails because an ion is surrounded by water and cannot leave that shell to enter a nonpolar interior, and the belief that the layer is an open sieve fails because phospholipids pack tightly against one another.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the molecule is water-hating, and what that does to the middle.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Surface Area to Volume Limits a Cell
questions.learningObjective: compute a cell's surface area to volume ratio and read its consequence
questions.stem: A spherical cell has a radius of 5 micrometres and is treated as a perfect sphere, with surface area 4 pi r squared and volume four thirds pi r cubed. What is its surface area divided by its volume, expressed per micrometre and rounded to two decimal places?

options.text: 0.17 per micrometre
options.misconception: divides the area by six times the radius

options.text: 0.60 per micrometre
1.20 per micrometre
options.misconception: uses the diameter in place of the radius

options.text: 1.67 per micrometre
options.misconception: inverts the ratio to give volume over area

questions.explanation: The area is 4 pi times 25, which is 314.2, and the volume is four thirds pi times 125, which is 523.6, so 314.2 divided by 523.6 is 0.60 per micrometre. Canceling the pi terms gives 3 divided by the radius, and 3 divided by 5 is 0.60, so both routes agree. The tempting wrong belief that the answer is volume over area fails because that ratio is 1.67 and rises with size, whereas the exchange of materials depends on the area per unit of volume, which is why a small cell is at the advantage.
questions.hint: Cancel pi and the powers of r before substituting numbers.

questions.topic: Cumulative: What a Steroid Ring Does in a Membrane
questions.learningObjective: connect a steroid's shape to its effect on membrane fluidity
questions.stem: A small fraction of a cell membrane is made of a steroid with a rigid four-ring core that sits between the fatty-acid tails. What does that accomplish when the cell is warm?

options.text: It limits how far the tails can spread, so the membrane resists fluidising
It pushes the tails apart, so the membrane grows more fluid when warm
options.misconception: reverses the effect of a rigid ring on tail movement

options.text: It forms a channel across the bilayer for small polar solutes
options.misconception: turns a lipid into a transport protein

options.text: It stiffens the outer face alone, leaving the inner face fully fluid
options.misconception: restricts a whole-membrane effect to one leaflet

questions.hint: Ask what a rigid ring does to the freedom of the tails around it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Four Subunits and Cooperative Binding
questions.learningObjective: name the structural level that produces cooperative binding
questions.stem: A transport protein is built from four separately folded chains packed together, and once oxygen binds on one chain the other three take it up more readily. Which description covers both the structure and the behaviour?

options.text: Quaternary structure, and binding is cooperative across the four chains
Tertiary structure, and binding is cooperative across the four chains
options.misconception: names the level of one chain instead of the assembly

options.text: Primary structure, and binding is cooperative across the four chains
options.misconception: credits the amino acid sequence with a four-chain effect

options.text: Quaternary structure, and each of the four chains binds independently
options.misconception: keeps the right level but denies the mutual effect

questions.hint: Ask how many chains are in the working unit, and whether they help each other.

questions.learningObjective: read a described diagram of an enzyme closing on its substrate
questions.stem: A diagram draws an enzyme as two rounded lobes with a cleft between them, with a small substrate sitting in that cleft. options.text: The active site closes around the substrate, which is the idea of induced fit
The active site opens to release the product, which is the idea of induced fit
options.misconception: reads a closing cleft as a site that has just emptied

options.text: Two separate enzymes have joined permanently to make one larger one

options.misconception: reads a narrower cleft as evidence of cleavage

questions.topic: Cumulative: One Amino Acid, One Sticky Surface
questions.learningObjective: link a single residue change to a surface property of a folded protein
questions.stem: A single amino acid in a large transport protein is changed, and the folded protein now presents a sticky patch on its surface so that many proteins clump together, deforming the cells that carry them. Which structural level does that change act through?

options.text: Tertiary structure, since the surface patch follows from how one chain folds
Primary structure alone, since the change is one altered amino acid
options.misconception: believes the sequence change cannot alter the folded surface

options.text: Quaternary structure, since the patch forms where four chains meet
options.misconception: assigns a single-chain effect to an assembly of chains

options.text: Primary structure, since the sequence change cannot reach the outside of the protein
options.misconception: keeps the right level but denies the folding link

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Translating Only Part of a Message
questions.learningObjective: calculate the untranslated part of a messenger RNA
questions.stem: A messenger RNA is 1,200 nucleotides long and is read from its first base, producing a protein of 180 amino acids with the stop codon at the end of those 180. How many nucleotides at the far end of the message are never translated into amino acids?

options.text: 540 nucleotides
options.misconception: reports the translated part as if it were the unused part

options.text: 720 nucleotides
options.misconception: multiplies the residues by four instead of three

options.text: 1,200 nucleotides
options.misconception: claims the whole message is left untranslated

options.text: 660 nucleotides

questions.explanation: Each residue occupies three nucleotides, so 180 residues use 540 nucleotides, and 1,200 minus 540 is 660 that are never read into the protein, which is what an untranslated region at the far end of a message is for. Counting codons instead of residues agrees: 1,200 divided by 3 is 400 codons, of which 180 are used, leaving 220 codons, and 220 times 3 is 660. The tempting wrong belief that 540 is the unused part fails because that is the figure for the part that is used, and treating four nucleotides per residue fails because a codon is three bases long.
questions.hint: Work out how much of the message is used, then subtract from the total.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Wall, Water and Turgor
questions.learningObjective: connect cellulose wall structure to turgor pressure
questions.stem: A plant cell has taken in water until it is firm and pressing outward against a rigid cellulose wall outside its membrane. What is that pressing force called, and what is the wall's part in it?

options.text: Turgor pressure, and the wall resists it so the cell stays firm not swollen
Osmotic pressure, and the wall adds to it until the cell splits open
options.misconception: names a related pressure and denies the wall's restraint

options.text: Turgor pressure, and without the wall the cell would take in water endlessly
options.misconception: keeps the right term but says the wall does no work

options.text: Blood pressure, and the wall pushes water inward to refill the cell
options.misconception: borrows a circulatory term for a plant cell

questions.explanation: Water inside the cell pushes on the membrane, the membrane pushes on the wall, and the wall pushes back, so the cell becomes firm, and that firmness is turgor, which is what keeps a plant upright and what stops a walled cell from bursting. questions.hint: Separate the pull that brings the water in from the push it then makes.

questions.topic: Cumulative: A Gradient Turned Directly into ATP
questions.learningObjective: link proton flow through a membrane channel to ATP synthesis
questions.stem: An enzyme sits in a membrane with a stalk and a rounded head, and the head only turns when protons flow past it through the membrane from a region of higher to lower proton concentration. What does that flow drive?

options.text: Building ATP from ADP and phosphate, using the gradient as its energy source
Pumping protons back up the gradient, using the turning head as its source
options.misconception: reverses the flow that the gradient produces

options.text: Splitting water into protons and oxygen inside the membrane
options.misconception: puts a photosynthetic reaction inside a respiratory channel

options.text: Transporting glucose across the membrane, using the turning head as a motor
options.misconception: makes a proton channel a glucose transporter

questions.topic: Cumulative: Why a Water Channel Speeds Up Osmosis
questions.learningObjective: explain how a channel protein raises the rate of water movement
questions.stem: A membrane protein forms a short tunnel lined with polar groups, and water crosses the membrane through it far faster than it would through the lipid layer alone. How does the tunnel achieve that?

options.text: It offers polar groups that water can hydrogen-bond to as it passes through
It is water-hating inside, so water is squeezed through at high pressure
options.misconception: makes the channel lining repel the molecule it transports

options.text: It uses energy from ATP to pump water in against the concentration gradient
options.misconception: calls an aquaporin an energy-driven pump

options.text: It binds water permanently and later releases it into the cytoplasm
options.misconception: makes a channel a permanent store of water

Solute being pumped uphill through the channel, which costs energy from ATP

options.text: Water being pulled out of the cell by the protein, leaving the cell shrinking

options.misconception: treats a protein channel as a hole torn in the membrane

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: What a Small Change in pH Does to a Buffer
questions.learningObjective: read a buffer ratio from a small change in pH
questions.stem: A patient's arterial pH is 7.40 and later the same sample reads 6.40. A buffer holds its hydrogen-ion concentration down, and one whole unit of pH is one factor of ten in the hydrogen-ion concentration. By what factor does the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbonic acid change between the two readings?

options.text: It rises ten-fold
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the ratio when pH falls

options.text: It falls ten-fold
It falls a hundred-fold
options.misconception: treats a one-unit fall as two orders of magnitude

options.text: It does not change at all
options.misconception: believes a buffer holds a ratio perfectly constant

questions.explanation: The pH has fallen by exactly one unit, and one unit on this scale is one order of magnitude, so the hydrogen-ion concentration has risen by a factor of ten and the ratio of base to acid has fallen by the same factor of ten, which is what lets a buffer shift the ratio in a controlled way rather than not at all. The tempting belief that a fall of only one tenth of a unit would already be ten-fold fails because a tenth of a unit is a factor of about 1.26, so the size of the change in the ratio is set by how many whole units the pH has moved.
questions.hint: One pH unit is one order of magnitude, so scale the change.

questions.learningObjective: trace a water shortage through stomata, carbon fixation and sugar supply
questions.stem: A week of no rain leaves the soil dry, and in the days that follow the plant's sugar production falls even though the days are long and sunny. Which chain of consequences accounts for that?

options.text: Stomata close, so less carbon dioxide enters and less sugar is fixed
Stomata close, so the plant stops taking in oxygen and cannot make sugar
options.misconception: credits oxygen rather than carbon dioxide for sugar making

options.misconception: makes long bright days the limiting factor in dry soil

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Tracing a Block in Respiration
questions.learningObjective: trace a block early in respiration through the carrier chain and ATP output
questions.stem: A drug stops the enzyme that converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA. Oxygen is still plentiful, yet the cell's ATP supply falls well below normal. Which explanation connects the block to the loss of ATP?

options.text: The cycle downstream is starved of fuel, so fewer carriers are loaded and reoxidised
The cycle makes oxygen, so blocking pyruvate removes the cell's oxygen supply
options.misconception: claims the cycle produces the oxygen that respiration uses

options.text: Electrons cannot leave the carriers, so they build up until the chain stops entirely
options.misconception: locates the block at the terminal acceptor instead of upstream

options.text: The cell cannot make water without acetyl-CoA, so the membranes dry out
options.misconception: treats the end product water as the whole problem

questions.topic: Cumulative: Tracing a Hormone to Glucose Entry
questions.learningObjective: trace a hormonal signal to a change in membrane transport
questions.stem: A muscle cell takes in far more glucose after a hormone is released into the blood, even though the glucose concentration outside the cell is unchanged. Which chain best explains that increase?

options.text: Signalling moves carrier vesicles to the surface, so more glucose channels are present
Signalling widens the pores in the membrane, so glucose leaks further in
options.misconception: makes the membrane leaky rather than adding carriers

options.text: Signalling destroys the cell's glycogen, so the extra glucose comes from inside
options.misconception: confuses an uptake effect with a breakdown of stored sugar

options.text: Signalling raises the outside concentration, so more glucose moves in by diffusion

questions.topic: Cumulative: Reading a Leaf's Gas Changes Over a Day
questions.learningObjective: interpret gas changes as the balance of two processes
questions.stem: A leaf is kept in a sealed jar with a lamp. During the lit hours the carbon dioxide in the jar falls and the oxygen rises, and through the dark hours both move back the other way. Which account fits that pattern?

options.text: In the light the carbon-fixing process exceeds respiration, and in the dark only respiration runs
The light makes the leaf take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen all night as well

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Why Recessive Conditions Rise in a Small Group
questions.learningObjective: explain how small population size raises the chance of recessive disease
questions.stem: A condition caused by a single recessive allele is rare in a large population but appears in about one birth in fifty in a small isolated group where relatives are common. Explain why, using what happens to allele frequencies when a population stays small.

answer.exemplar: An individual shows a recessive condition only when both copies of the gene carry the allele, so the condition appears where two carriers meet, and in a large population carriers are spread thinly and rarely meet each other. In a small group, chance events remove a few individuals at random, and because the allele is rare those few are more likely to be the ones carrying it than anyone else, so the frequency of the allele among the survivors rises by luck alone. As that frequency climbs, carriers become a larger share of the group, two carriers meet more often by chance, and the condition becomes common, all without any change in how the allele acts. Second, small populations drift: random loss of individuals moves allele frequencies by chance, and rare alleles are the ones most often lost or, in a founder group, most often over-represented.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Design a Test of a Nutrient Effect
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled field test of a nutrient effect on growth
questions.stem: A farmer suspects that adding a nitrogen fertiliser to one field raises the yield of the crop. Describe an experiment that could test this, and name at least two things other than the fertiliser that must be kept the same.

answer.exemplar: Split the land into plots of the same size, grow the same crop at the same density in every plot, and apply the fertiliser to some randomly chosen plots and none to others, so that any difference in yield cannot be blamed on which patch of ground happened to be used. Water the plots identically, harvest them on the same day, and weigh the dry yield per plot rather than judging by eye. Two things that must be held constant are the amount of water and the seed density, and a third is the soil, which is why several plots rather than one are needed. The essential comparison is between the treated and untreated plots within the same field and season, because a single treated plot compared with a neighbouring field would confound the fertiliser with soil, water and management differences.

Without the untreated plots there is nothing to compare yield against, and without random assignment the treated plots may simply have been the better ground, which is the failure mode this design is built to avoid.

questions.topic: Cumulative: Design a Test That Separates Two Mechanisms
questions.learningObjective: design measurements that distinguish a direct effect from a killing effect
questions.stem: A compound stops an enzyme working in a test tube, and the same compound also stops bacteria growing. Describe an experiment that could show whether the growth effect is caused by blocking that enzyme or by killing the bacteria outright, and say what each result would mean.

If the enzyme's rate in the extract falls in step with the concentration, and the bacteria stop dividing well before they show signs of damage, then blocking the enzyme is the earlier event and the growth effect is explained by it. If the bacteria show damage and lose viability at concentrations too low to inhibit the enzyme measurably, the growth effect is a killing effect and the enzyme result is a coincidence of that concentration range. questions.explanation: Separating two mechanisms needs a measurement for each, at the same range of concentrations, plus a control that removes one mechanism from the picture. A knockout strain or a cell-free system is the decisive control here, because it lets the two candidate explanations give different predictions rather than both merely being consistent with the data.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: Why a Control and a Repeat Are Both Needed
questions.learningObjective: explain the separate jobs of a control and a repeated measurement
questions.stem: Two rules are quoted for any experiment: include a control and repeat the measurement. Explain what each rule is for, and why doing only one of them still leaves a result untrustworthy.

answer.exemplar: They guard against two different mistakes. The control answers the question of what would have happened anyway, because without a comparison the result could be due to something other than the treatment: the water was warm, the plant was dying, the soil was poor, the day was unusual. Repeats answer a different question, which is how much the result wobbles, because living systems vary and a single measurement cannot tell a real effect from the spread of ordinary variation. Doing only the control leaves a result that may be a fluke repeated faithfully, and doing only the repeats leaves a result that may be consistent and entirely caused by something the experiment never varied, since consistency is not causation. The tempting belief that many repeats make an uncontrolled result safe fails because repeating the same flawed comparison reproduces the same flaw, and the belief that one well-chosen control is enough fails because a control cannot reveal variation within a group.

questions.explanation: The two rules are independent safeguards. A control fixes the comparison by holding everything else the same, and repeats fix the uncertainty by showing the spread, and an experiment missing either one has a different and unfixable weakness, which is why neither substitutes for the other.
questions.hint: Ask what failure a control prevents, and what failure a repeat prevents.

questions.topic: Cumulative: From a Molecule to a Community
questions.learningObjective: explain how one molecular change can scale up to a community effect
questions.stem: A single amino acid change in a photosynthetic enzyme reduces the carbon a plant fixes by a tenth, and in a region where that plant is the main food source, animal numbers fall within a year. answer.exemplar: The chain runs through nested levels. The residue changes the shape of the active site, so the reaction it catalyses is slower, so each plant fixes less carbon, so the plant grows more slowly and stores less sugar in its tissues. A plant that is a main food source then supplies less energy to every animal above it, and because the animals also reproduce less well when fed less, the effect carries up the food web rather than fading out. What stops it spreading is any compensating link: other food sources, a species that eats something else, a reservoir of stored carbon, or the fact that a gene is usually present in only part of a population, in which case plants with a normal copy keep growing and the effect is diluted. The tempting belief that one residue can only change one molecule fails because the molecule is a catalyst inside a leaf, and a leaf is food, and food is energy for everything that eats it, and the belief that the effect must be total fails because compensation is common and is exactly why a ten-fold loss of photosynthesis need not produce a ten-fold loss of animals.

questions.explanation: The item is about scale. A catalytic change is small in itself, but catalysts sit inside a food web, so the effect is transmitted through every feeding step, and the brakes on that transmission are compensation, alternative food sources, and how much of the population carries the change at all.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Cumulative: When a Small Change Does Not Scale Up
questions.learningObjective: explain why a small change sometimes has no large effect at higher levels
questions.stem: A change in one species' feeding rate does not produce the large change in plant abundance that a simple food web would suggest, and the web appears to hold steady. Explain what can absorb such a change so that the system does not move very far.

answer.exemplar: Several things can absorb such a change before it travels far. Another species that eats the same prey can rise to take its place, so the total grazing pressure on the resource is much the same. The resource itself usually has a floor it cannot be pushed below, and the consumer cannot keep eating once the resource is scarce, so the decline in the resource stops well short of extinction. The response can also be fast enough to catch the recovery, since a population whose food is increasing begins reproducing before the food has peaked, which damps the oscillation. Finally, individuals move towards better patches, so the change is spread thinly over the whole area rather than applied to one place at full strength. The tempting belief that a web is only a set of arrows fails because what matters is how many other links lead to the same resource, and the belief that a small change must produce a small change fails because the size of a response has to be measured rather than assumed from the size of the driver.

questions.explanation: Absorption is what keeps a web steady, and the mechanisms are worth naming: alternative consumers, a floor under the resource, a response fast enough to catch the recovery, and movement that spreads the change out. Each of these breaks the chain before a large change in plant abundance can develop, which is why the same web can absorb one change and amplify another.
questions.hint: Ask who else eats the same thing, and where the resource stops falling.
